n: Habakkuk ends with a prayer set to music, like a psalm. His questions have turned into worship.

f.g: A musical term of uncertain meaning, perhaps an emotional, wandering style of song (see Psalm 7 heading).

n: Habakkuk is awed by what God has revealed. He asks the Lord to renew His mighty works in their own day — and, in wrath, to remember mercy.

f.g: Renew Your saving deeds, as in the past.

n: Habakkuk recalls God marching from the south, from Teman and Mount Paran, as when He came to Israel at Sinai. His glory fills the heavens.

f.g: A region in Edom, south of Judah.
A musical or liturgical marker, perhaps meaning a pause.

n: His brightness is like sunlight, with rays flashing from His hand — and still that is only the hiding place of His full power.

f.g: Rays of light (the same Hebrew word as for horns).
Even this blinding light veils His full power.

n: Plague and fiery bolts go before and after Him, as in the plagues of Egypt.
He stands and the earth shakes; nations scatter and ancient mountains crumble. His ways are eternal.
Desert peoples — Cushan and Midian — trembled in their tents when God came.

f.g: Probably a tribe related to Midian, in the southern wilderness.

n: Was God angry with the rivers and sea when He rode out in His chariots of salvation? Habakkuk recalls the parting of the Red Sea and the Jordan.
God uncovered His bow, fulfilling His sworn promises, and split the earth with rivers.

f.w: according to the oaths of the tribes, even thy word
f.g: One of the hardest lines in the Old Testament to translate; perhaps “arrows sworn by Your word.”

n: The mountains writhed, torrents swept by, and the deep roared and lifted its waves like hands.

f.w: The mountains saw thee, and they trembled

n: Sun and moon stood still at the flash of His arrows and spear — recalling Joshua’s long day.

f.w: The sun and moon stood still

n: In anger God marched through the earth and trampled the nations like grain on a threshing floor.
God went out to save His people and His anointed, crushing the leader of the wicked and laying him bare from head to foot.

f.g: Hebrew mashiaḥ — the anointed king, or Israel itself; Christians see a hint of the Messiah.

f.w: discovering the foundation unto the neck
f.g: Stripping him bare from foundation to neck.

n: God turned the enemy’s own weapons against them. They had rushed in like a storm to scatter God’s people, gloating like those who devour the helpless in secret.
God trampled the sea with His horses, churning the great waters, as at the Exodus.

f.w: Thou didst walk through the sea

n: Hearing all this, Habakkuk trembles to his bones. Yet he will wait quietly for the day of trouble to come on the invaders.

f.g: His strength drained away from fear.

n: One of scripture’s great expressions of faith: even if the fig tree, vines, olives, fields, flocks, and herds all fail — every source of livelihood gone —

f.w: the fig tree shall not blossom

n: — yet I will rejoice in the Lord and find joy in the God who saves me. Faith does not depend on circumstances. Habakkuk moves from “How long?” to “Yet I will rejoice.”

f.w: Yet I will rejoice in the LORD

n: The Lord gives strength and makes Habakkuk sure-footed as a deer on mountain heights — able to stand firm in hard places. The note at the end directs the song to the choir leader.

f.w: he will make my feet like hinds' feet

f.g: Female deer, famously sure-footed on steep cliffs.
The music director, as in many psalm headings.
